row.question:
Based on the chest X-ray findings, what is the most likely diagnosis for the mass observed in the left hemithorax of this asymptomatic 40-year-old man with no history of asbestos exposure? Consider the mass's contour, its angle with the thoracic wall, and the mediastinal shift.  
A) Malignant mesothelioma  
B) Pleural lipoma  
C) Intercostal schwannoma  
D) Fibrous tumor of the pleura  
E) Askin tumor  
F) Pleural fibrosarcoma

reflection_candidates.json.condition: When mediastinal opacity obscures one heart border and tracheal deviation is present on PA CXR
reflection_candidates.json.action: Inspect which cardiac border is silhouetted (left border loss = left mediastinal pathology; right border loss = right-sided) and confirm tracheal deviation direction—deviation away from mass side—and compare costophrenic angle blunting severity per side.
reflection_candidates.json.limitation: Unreliable if both borders obscured or in severe cardiomegaly; requires adequate inspiration and centering.

reflection_candidates.json.condition: When a round-oval opacity obscures a cardiophrenic angle on PA CXR and appears smaller on lateral view
reflection_candidates.json.action: Inspect lateral CXR for whether the opacity lies anterior to the cardiac silhouette (suggesting anterior mediastinal/chest wall origin) versus overlapping the spine (posterior); anterior masses are foreshortened laterally
reflection_candidates.json.limitation: Unreliable if cardiac borders are poorly visualized or if mass is small (<2 cm)
